motion: Do we need God for morality?

items.currentText: Initially described morality through desire and belief before fully supplying a correctness standard.
items.lockedProposition: Morality does not require God; its operative package requires a desire to do good and a belief about what is good.

items.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Dillahunty immediately contests divine necessity by separating motivation from grounding and identifying desire plus belief as operationally sufficient ingredients for recognizable moral conduct. Principal limitation: This formulation risks defining morality through the psychology of agents without yet explaining what makes their beliefs correct or why desired goodness possesses authority beyond preference which Ferrer expressly disputes. Live burden: He must supplement the practical package with a defensible standard for evaluating mistaken desires and beliefs while showing that such evaluation remains genuinely moral rather than merely instrumental coordination.

items.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: The chess analogy separates uncertainty from arbitrariness: invented rules and avoiding defeat still make positions and sequences objectively better, even when players cannot identify the optimal move. Principal limitation: Chess supplies bounded rules, determinate outcome, shared participation, whereas the excerpt establishes neither a precise moral goal nor a method for comparing interpersonal consequences and rival improvements. Live burden: Dillahunty must show that morality has shared ends and evaluative constraints for comparable goal-relative objectivity, especially when disagreement concerns the governing goal itself rather than incomplete knowledge about which means advances it.
